newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: FEATURE-Guns and glamor - women rebels fight Colombian war.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Guns and glamor - women rebels fight Colombian war.

text.p: The nail-polish is chipped on her trigger finger, an automatic assault rifle hangs from her shoulder and her lean figure is hidden under bulky combat fatigues. Patricia gives a new twist to the term "femme fatale."
The 22-year-old guerrilla is one of hundreds of women in the ranks of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), Latin America's oldest and largest rebel army.

"The fact that we're here in the guerrilla should serve to show other women that they're capable of fighting," she told Reuters during the first visit by journalists to the base camp of the FARC's Southern Bloc in the jungles of southern Caqueta province. "If women do not want to join and pick up a gun then they should organise themselves in other ways."

One insurgent tentatively estimated that about 20 percent of the FARC's fighters were women. No exact figures are available but for Joaquin Gomez, the commander of the Southern Bloc, the role of women in the "people's war" is fundamental.
"A woman is more sensitive than a man because she perceives injustice through every pore in her body. From the moment she is born she is discriminated against," he said.

According to government statistics, that discrimination translates into wages on average 66 percent lower for women than for their male counterparts and illiteracy levels almost 6 percent higher among Colombian women than men.
ASSAULT RIFLES AND LIP-GLOSS

Throughout the sprawling rebel camp young women warriors polished their high-powered assault rifles -- Israeli-made Galils, U.S.-made R-15s and Russian or Chinese-built Kalashnikovs -- and checked their ammo pouches.

Equality in the ranks means they must take their turn alongside the men cooking for their comrades-in-arms. And they too must battle through the mud and dense jungle undergrowth with as much as 45 pounds (20 kg) of food and equipment in home-made backpacks.

Despite the tough conditions living in the intense humidity of the jungle and fighting a hit-and-run war, the peasant daughters turned revolutionaries like to keep up appearances. With the aid of small hand-held mirrors they paint on eyeliner or lip-gloss and drag wide-toothed combs through their thick black hair. They add an individual touch to their bush hats with multicolored shoelaces or tie bright hair-bands around the handles of their machetes.
But when the shooting starts there is no distinction between the genders.

Sonia, 25, took part in last August's attack on the Las Delicias military base in neighbouring Putumayo province. The FARC, set up as a pro-Soviet force in 1964, killed 31 soldiers and took 60 prisoner in one of the FARC's greatest politico- military victories in its 33-year-old uprising. The prisoners were released more than nine months later on June 15.
NO FEAR UNDER FIRE

"I wasn't afraid when I went into that battle. I was ready for it. We were sure we were going to win," Sonia said. "Everybody knows they could die at any time but at least we're fighting for change," she added, explaining that she joined the rebels to fight against the "discrimination of women in Colombian society."

Her colleague Argenis, 19, who joined the FARC when she was just 13, added: "Maybe at the start you're frightened. But after the first few shots you react, take up positions and get your fear under control."

Unlike many regular armies throughout the world, this "people's army" does not frown on love in a time of war. But Sonia was quick to say there was no promiscuity and even less free love. Male and female guerrillas begin a relationship only after seeking permission from their immediate superiors.

Both partners take an equal responsibility for birth control, the rebels say. "The man and the woman use contraceptives. After all we're taking part in the armed struggle and everything must be done under strict control," Argenis said.

Gladys' route into the FARC was somewhat unorthodox. She says she was sent by the army to infiltrate the guerrillas after receiving three months of training in torture techniques from an army pilot in provincial capital Florencia.
"We pulled (our victims') eyes out alive with needles ... and cut off their testicles. Some days the (instructors) brought us 12 or 13 people," she said.
Her life was spared after a full admission of guilt at a rebel court-martial and she was admitted to the ranks.
While none of the female fighters appeared to regret their decision to take up arms for the overthrow of the "bourgeois state" some undoubtedly look forward to the day that they can start a family.
"We must wait for a family because we have decided to be here. The armed struggle and the changes we're fighting for must come first," Patricia said.
